source: regulator / gazette / official platform policy pages read 2026-10-04; law-firm or news summaries named as such in notes

items.name: ASCI Guidelines for Influencer Advertising in Digital Media (incl. virtual influencers, health and finance influencers)
items.one_line: Every influencer post with any material connection to the brand must carry an upfront disclosure label; virtual influencers must say they are not human; finance and health influencers must state qualifications.

sources.title: ASCI: Guidelines for Influencer Advertising in Digital Media (with Addendum I 15.07.2021 and Addendum II 17.08.2023)
sources.supports: full text: disclosure criteria, placement, permitted labels, video timing, virtual influencers, due diligence, health/BFSI qualifications

sources.title: ASCI press release: final Guidelines for Influencer Advertising
sources.supports: guidelines apply to posts published on or after 14 June 2021

items.note: In force since 14 June 2021; Addendum II (health and finance influencers) dated 17 Aug 2023 (read in the PDF 2026-10-04). Rules: (1) disclose whenever there is ANY material connection, including free or discounted products, even if the review is honest (guideline 1.1). (2) Permitted labels only: Advertisement, Ad, Sponsored, Collaboration, Partnership, Employee, Free gift, Affiliate, Instagram 'Paid Partnership' tag, YouTube 'Includes Paid Promotion' tag; in English or the ad's own language (1.3). (3) Upfront and prominent: not only in bio, not at the end, not behind MORE, not buried in hashtags; platform tool is in addition to, not instead of, your own label (1.2). (4) Picture/video posts with no text: superimpose the label; video <=15 s: label >=3 s; 15 s to 2 min: 1/3 of length; >=2 min: whole section where the brand is discussed; live streams: announce at start and end; audio: start, end and around every break (1.2e-g). (5) Virtual influencer must additionally disclose upfront that the audience is not interacting with a real human (1.4). (6) BFSI stock/investment talk: SEBI registration number stated with name; other finance: IRDAI licence, CA, CS etc.; health/nutrition: medical degree, nurse, dietician etc.; qualification shown upfront (Addendum II). Both advertiser and influencer are responsible (1.5).

items.name: FTC Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising (16 CFR Part 255, revised 2023)
items.one_line: US rule set for influencer and testimonial copy: honest opinions only, no claims the brand could not make itself, and a clear, unavoidable disclosure of any material connection.

sources.title: eCFR: 16 CFR Part 255 Guides Concerning Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising
sources.supports: current text of the Guides

sources.title: FTC: Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers
sources.supports: plain-language disclosure rules for influencers: placement, wording, video and live

sources.title: FTC: FTC's Endorsement Guides: What People Are Asking
sources.supports: FAQ on material connections, affiliate links, reviews, platform tools

items.note: Revised Guides adopted by the FTC in June 2023 and in force (eCFR current text, checked 2026-10-04). For a copywriter: (1) an endorsement must reflect the endorser's honest opinion and cannot convey a claim the advertiser could not substantiate itself (Part 255). (2) Any material connection (payment, free product, family/employment, affiliate commission) must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously, i.e. hard to miss, in the endorsement itself, not only on a profile page (Disclosures 101). (3) Use simple, clear words like 'advertisement', 'ad', 'sponsored'; 'Don't use vague or confusing terms like "sp," "spon," or "collab,"' and 'Don't assume that a platform's disclosure tool is good enough' (Disclosures 101). (4) In video, say it in the video, not just the description; in live streams, repeat it periodically (Disclosures 101). Penalty figures not taken from memory: check the FTC page before quoting any.

items.name: FTC Trade Regulation Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials (16 CFR Part 465, 2024)
items.one_line: Bans fake or AI-invented reviews and testimonials, bought reviews, undisclosed insider reviews, review suppression and fake social-media indicators such as bought followers or views.

sources.title: FTC press release: Federal Trade Commission Announces Final Rule Banning Fake Reviews and Testimonials (14 Aug 2024)
sources.supports: what the rule bans, including AI-generated fake reviews and fake social media indicators

sources.title: eCFR: 16 CFR Part 465 Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials
sources.supports: rule text

items.note: Final rule announced 14 Aug 2024 by a 5-0 vote; 'effective 60 days after the date it's published in the Federal Register' (FTC release read 2026-10-04; widely reported as 21 Oct 2024, not re-checked in the Federal Register). Rules from the FTC release: (1) no reviews or testimonials that misrepresent that they are by someone who does not exist, 'such as AI-generated fake reviews', or by someone with no actual experience of the product. (2) Insider reviews by officers, managers, employees or agents need clear and conspicuous disclosure of the connection. (3) No review suppression by threats or intimidation. (4) No buying or selling 'fake indicators of social media influence, such as followers or views generated by a bot or hijacked account'. Civil penalties apply to knowing violators.

items.name: CAN-SPAM Act (US commercial email)
items.one_line: US law for commercial email: honest headers and subject lines, the message identified as an ad, a physical postal address, and a working opt-out honoured promptly.

sources.title: FTC: CAN-SPAM Act: A Compliance Guide for Business
sources.supports: the main requirements, opt-out timing, liability of the sender and the hired agency

items.note: In force since 2004 (FTC guide read 2026-10-04). Rules quoted from the guide: (1) no false or misleading header information; (2) 'The subject line must accurately reflect the content of the message'; (3) 'disclose clearly and conspicuously that your message is an advertisement'; (4) include 'your valid physical postal address'; (5) opt-out must work for at least 30 days after sending and be honoured 'within 10 business days', with no fee or extra data demanded. You 'can't contract away your legal responsibility' by hiring an agency; the guide gives penalties of up to $53,088 per violating email (inflation-adjusted, re-check before quoting).

items.name: COPPA Rule (Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule, 16 CFR Part 312)
items.one_line: US rule for sites, apps and channels directed to children under 13: no collecting their personal information without verifiable parental consent.

sources.title: eCFR: 16 CFR Part 312 Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule
sources.supports: rule text

sources.title: FTC: Complying with COPPA: Frequently Asked Questions
sources.supports: when content is 'directed to children', obligations of channel owners

items.note: In force; amended rule finalised by the FTC in 2025 (see the FTC COPPA page for the amendment's effective and compliance dates; not confirmed here). Copy rules: (1) if content is directed to under-13s, do not write CTAs that collect personal information (comments with names, sign-ups, contests) without verifiable parental consent; (2) on YouTube, kids content must be set 'made for kids', which limits comments and personalised ads (FTC FAQ). Treat any kids brief for a US audience as a legal review item.

items.name: IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026: synthetically generated information
items.one_line: India's 2026 IT Rules amendment: realistic AI-generated or altered audio, images and video ('synthetically generated information') must carry a prominent label and provenance metadata, big platforms must make uploaders declare it, and takedown clocks drop to hours.

sources.title: MeitY: IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 [updated as on 10.02.2026]
sources.supports: rule 2(1)(wa) SGI definition and exclusions; rule 3(3) labelling and metadata; rule 4(1A) SSMI user declaration; 3-hour and 2-hour takedown substitutions by G.S.R. 120(E) dated 10.02.2026

sources.title: Gazette of India: G.S.R. 120(E), IT Amendment Rules, 2026
sources.supports: official gazette notification

sources.title: MeitY: draft IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules, 2026 (March 2026, date blank)
sources.supports: a further amendment was in draft in March 2026 (intermediaries to follow MeitY advisories/SOPs)

sources.title: Freshfields (law firm summary): key changes under MeitY's 2026 amendments
sources.supports: in force 20 Feb 2026

items.note: Notified by G.S.R. 120(E) dated 10 Feb 2026; in force 20 Feb 2026 (Freshfields, law-firm summary; MeitY consolidated text read 2026-10-04). A Second Amendment was only a draft in March 2026; its status was not confirmed. Rules for a creator: (1) SGI = audio, visual or audio-visual content artificially created or altered so that it appears real and a person or event looks indistinguishable from reality (rule 2(1)(wa)); text-only copy is outside it; routine good-faith editing, colour/noise fixes, templates and accessibility or translation edits that do not change meaning are excluded. (2) Lawful SGI must be 'prominently labelled' so it is easy to notice, or carry a 'prominently prefixed audio disclosure' for audio, plus permanent metadata/identifier where technically feasible; the label must not be removable (rule 3(3)). (3) SGI that falsely shows a real person's identity, voice, conduct or statement, or a real event, in a way likely to deceive, falls in the class platforms must block (rule 3(3)(a)(i)(IV)): no realistic fake quotes or fake events of real people, even as satire, unless clearly unreal and labelled. (4) On significant social media intermediaries the uploader must declare whether content is SGI and the platform must verify it (rule 4(1A)). (5) Government/court takedown window is now three hours (was 36 hours), so contested content disappears fast.

items.name: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and DPDP Rules, 2025
items.one_line: India's data protection law: personal data (including phone numbers and emails used for marketing) needs specific consent through a clear, separate notice; children's data needs verifiable parental consent.

sources.title: PIB explainer (17 Nov 2025): DPDP Rules, 2025 Notified
sources.supports: Rules notified 14 Nov 2025; eighteen-month phased compliance; separate clear consent notice with specific purpose; verifiable parental consent for children; penalty ceilings

sources.title: Lexology (law-firm summary): DPDP Rules, 2025: operationalising consent, security and governance obligations
sources.supports: phase dates: Rules 1, 2, 17-21 at once; consent managers about Nov 2026; main obligations about May 2027

items.note: Act enacted 11 Aug 2023; Rules notified 14 Nov 2025 with an eighteen-month phased compliance period (PIB, read 2026-10-04). Per law-firm summaries (medium confidence) the core notice and consent duties bite from about May 2027 and consent-manager registration from about Nov 2026: so as of 2026-10-04 most duties are announced but not yet enforceable. Copy rules: (1) every lead form or opt-in needs a separate consent notice, 'clear and easy to understand', stating the specific purpose (PIB). (2) Purpose-specific consent: a purchase or a download is not consent to marketing. (3) Children's data needs verifiable parental consent (PIB), so no data-capturing CTAs aimed at kids. (4) Penalty ceilings in the Act are high (PIB lists up to Rs 250 crore for security failures, up to Rs 200 crore for breach-notice or children's violations, up to Rs 50 crore for other violations).

items.name: Election Commission of India directions on labelling AI-generated / synthetic campaign content (Jan 2025, Oct 2025, Apr 2026)
items.one_line: ECI requires parties, candidates and campaigners to label AI-generated or digitally altered campaign images, audio and video, name who made it, and remove misleading synthetic content within three hours.

sources.title: All India Radio News (16 Jan 2025): ECI directs political parties to label AI-generated synthetic content in campaigns
sources.supports: Jan 2025 advisory and label wording

sources.title: All India Radio News (25 Oct 2025): EC issues fresh guidelines on AI and synthetic content use in Bihar poll campaigns
sources.supports: Oct 2025 advisory

sources.title: Business Today (24 Oct 2025): ECI mandates clear labelling of AI generated content in political campaigns
sources.supports: label covers at least 10% of visible area, top of screen for video, first 10% of audio, creator named, 3-hour takedown, records

sources.title: MediaNama (Apr 2026): ECI orders 3-hour takedown rule for AI and fake content in elections
sources.supports: 22 Apr 2026 directions for Assam, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, West Bengal polls; label wording plus originating entity

items.note: Advisories dated Jan 2025 and 24 Oct 2025, reiterated 22 Apr 2026 for the 2026 assembly polls (news reports of ECI/PIB releases, read 2026-10-04; ECI's own PDF not read: medium confidence). Rules: (1) label every AI-generated or significantly altered campaign image, video or audio 'AI-Generated', 'Digitally Enhanced' or 'Synthetic Content'. (2) Per the Oct 2025 advisory the label should cover at least 10% of the visible display area, sit at the top of the screen for video, and occupy the first 10% of duration for audio (Business Today). (3) Disclose the entity responsible in metadata or caption. (4) Misleading synthetic content on party channels must come down within 3 hours of notice; parties keep records of AI material. (5) Never fabricate a rival leader's voice, face or statement: it also falls under comp:it_rules_sgi_2026.

items.name: ECI Model Code of Conduct, MCMC pre-certification of political ads, and social media instructions
items.one_line: During elections, every political ad on TV, radio, e-papers, bulk SMS, voice calls, websites and social media needs prior certification from the district or state Media Certification and Monitoring Committee (MCMC), and campaign speech is bound by the Model Code of Conduct.

sources.title: All India Radio News (21 Mar 2026): EC mandates pre-certification of political ads on electronic and digital media
sources.supports: media covered, District vs State MCMC, social media accounts in affidavit, social media spend statement within 75 days

sources.title: Business Standard (14 Oct 2025): ECI makes pre-certification mandatory for political ads on social media
sources.supports: same rule applied to the Oct-Nov 2025 Bihar polls

sources.title: Election Commission of India: Model Code of Conduct
sources.supports: MCC text and instructions (landing page; not read in this harvest)

items.note: Applied in every recent election, most recently by the ECI order reported 21 Mar 2026 for the 2026 assembly polls (AIR News, read 2026-10-04). Rules: (1) no political ad on any internet-based media or social media by a party or candidate without MCMC pre-certification; candidates apply to the District MCMC, state-headquartered parties to the State MCMC (AIR News). (2) Candidates declare their authentic social media accounts in the nomination affidavit, and parties report internet/social media campaign spend to ECI within 75 days of the poll (AIR News). (3) MCC rules on content (no appeals to caste or communal feelings, no criticism of private life, no unverified allegations) apply to digital posts too: read the ECI MCC text before writing campaign copy (primary not read here). Ghost-writing for a party during an election = get the MCMC certificate number before the post goes live.

items.name: YouTube paid product placements, endorsements and sponsorships policy
items.one_line: YouTube creators must tick the 'paid promotion' box for videos with paid product placement, endorsements or sponsorships, which shows the 'Includes paid promotion' label, and must still follow local law.

sources.title: YouTube Help: Paid product placements, endorsements and sponsorships
sources.supports: the disclosure checkbox, what counts as paid promotion, creator and brand responsibilities

items.note: Current policy page read 2026-10-04. Rules: (1) for branded content, sponsorships, endorsements or other commercial relationships, select the paid promotion option in video details; this 'adds a disclosure label that appears at the beginning of your video'. (2) Branded content must also comply with YouTube Community Guidelines and Google Ads policies, and 'You and the partners you work with are also responsible for understanding and complying with all applicable legal requirements'. (3) Age and geography restrictions for branded content appear only after selecting Yes under Paid promotion. ASCI accepts the 'Includes Paid Promotion' tag as a label (comp:asci_influencer); the FTC still wants the disclosure said in the video itself (comp:ftc_endorsement_guides).

items.name: YouTube disclosure of altered or synthetic content
items.one_line: Creators must tick 'AI use' at upload for realistic content that is generated or meaningfully altered with AI (fake words or acts of a real person, altered real events or places, realistic scenes that never happened, AI music as the main focus); YouTube then labels it.

sources.title: YouTube Help: Disclosing use of altered or synthetic content
sources.supports: when disclosure is required and when it is not (clearly unrealistic, minor edits, beauty filters)

items.note: Current policy page read 2026-10-04. Rules: (1) disclose GenAI content that 'Makes a real person appear to say or do something they didn't do', 'Alters footage of a real event or place', 'Generates a realistic scene that didn't actually occur' or 'Creates music that's the main focus of the video'; disclose via 'AI use' under Attributes in YouTube Studio. (2) No disclosure for clearly unrealistic content or minor edits: beauty, colour or lighting filters, AI help with outline, script, thumbnail, title or captions, idea generation, cloning ONE'S OWN voice for voice-overs or dubs. (3) YouTube may auto-label content made with its own AI tools, content with C2PA metadata, or content its systems detect; creators who consistently fail to disclose risk labels, removal or suspension from the Partner Program. (4) Disclosure 'won't limit a video's audience or impact its eligibility to earn money'. India adds a legal labelling duty (comp:it_rules_sgi_2026).

items.name: Google Search spam policies (scaled content abuse, site reputation abuse, and others)
items.one_line: Google demotes or removes pages made mainly to rank: mass-produced unhelpful pages (by AI or humans), third-party pages riding a host site's reputation, keyword stuffing, hidden text and doorway pages.

sources.title: Google Search Central: Spam policies for Google web search
sources.supports: definitions of scaled content abuse, site reputation abuse, keyword stuffing, doorway abuse, expired domain abuse

items.note: Scaled content abuse, site reputation abuse and expired domain abuse were added in March 2024 (Google Search Central); current page checked 2026-10-04. Rules: (1) never generate many pages 'for the primary purpose of manipulating search rankings and not helping users', no matter whether AI or humans made them. (2) Sponsored or third-party content published on a strong host site to exploit its ranking signals is site reputation abuse. (3) No keyword stuffing, hidden text or doorway pages. Sponsored articles should be marked and linked rel=sponsored/nofollow (see comp:google_ai_content_guidance for the AI side).

items.name: Google Search guidance on AI-generated content
items.one_line: Google ranks content on helpfulness, not on how it was produced; AI is fine, AI used mainly to manipulate rankings is spam.

sources.title: Google Search Central Blog (8 Feb 2023): Google Search's guidance about AI-generated content
sources.supports: appropriate use of AI is not against guidelines; automation to manipulate rankings is spam; consider 'Who, How, Why' disclosures

sources.title: Google Search Central: Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content
sources.supports: people-first content and the Who/How/Why questions

items.note: Guidance from Feb 2023, still linked from Search Central (checked 2026-10-04). Rules: (1) judge drafts on E-E-A-T style helpfulness, not on 'written by AI'; (2) using automation 'with the primary purpose of manipulating ranking' violates spam policies; (3) Google suggests telling readers how content was made (Who, How, Why) where they would reasonably expect it; (4) do not give an AI an author byline.

items.name: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 50: transparency for AI-generated content
items.one_line: Deployers who publish deepfakes, or AI-generated text meant to inform the public on matters of public interest, must disclose that it is AI-generated; providers must mark synthetic output machine-readably.

sources.title: EUR-Lex: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act)
sources.supports: Article 50 text and Article 113 dates of application

sources.title: artificialintelligenceact.eu (Future of Life Institute reference site): Article 50 Transparency Obligations
sources.supports: Art 50 text read 2026-10-04: deep-fake disclosure, public-interest text disclosure unless human review/editorial responsibility, satire/art limitation

items.note: Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026 under Article 113 (EUR-Lex; Art 50 text read 2026-10-04 on the reference site). Rules for writers serving EU audiences: (1) deployers of a deep fake (AI image, audio or video resembling real persons, objects, places or events that would falsely appear authentic) 'shall disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated'; for evidently artistic, creative, satirical or fictional work the duty is limited to disclosing it 'in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work' (Art 50(4)). (2) AI-generated or manipulated 'text which is published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest' must be disclosed, unless it 'has undergone a process of human review or editorial control' and someone holds editorial responsibility (Art 50(4)). (3) Disclosure must be clear and distinguishable at the latest at first exposure (Art 50(5)). (4) Providers must machine-mark synthetic output (Art 50(2)). The 2025-26 'Digital Omnibus' package proposed changes to AI Act timelines; whether Art 50 dates moved was NOT confirmed in this harvest.

items.name: ASCI Code for Self-Regulation of Advertising Content in India
items.one_line: India's self-regulatory ad code: ads must be truthful and substantiated, decent, not promote harmful products or situations, and fair to competitors.
aliases: Advertising Standards Council of India code

sources.title: ASCI: The ASCI Code
sources.supports: four chapters; Chapter I clause 1 substantiation; Chapter III children; Chapter IV clause 1.5 denigration, clause 3 imitation; page updated 29 Apr 2024

items.note: In force (page last updated 29 Apr 2024, read via fetch summary 2026-10-04). Four chapters: I Truthful and Honest Representation; II Non-offensive to Public; III Against Harmful Products/Services/Situations; IV Fair in Competition. Rules: (1) every claim about objectively ascertainable fact must be capable of substantiation, so write only claims the client can prove on paper (Ch I.1). (2) Comparative copy may compare but must not unfairly denigrate, attack or discredit competitors directly or by implication (Ch IV.1.5). (3) Do not imitate another advertiser's earlier layout, copy, slogans or visuals (Ch IV.3). (4) Ads aimed at children must not contain anything that could cause physical, mental or moral harm or encourage dangerous acts (Ch III). ASCI guidelines (influencer, AI labelling) sit on top of this Code. ASCI is self-regulatory, but its complaints are routinely escalated to CCPA/regulators.

items.name: ASCI Guidelines for Responsible Labelling of Synthetically Generated Content in Advertising (2026)
items.one_line: ASCI's risk-based AI rule for ads: fabricated AI testimonials, AI-exaggerated results and unconsented likenesses are banned even with a label; AI influencers, voice clones, fabricated settings and unbuilt products must be labelled; AI-written copy needs no label.

sources.title: ASCI: Guidelines for Responsible Labelling of Synthetically Generated Content in Advertising (Board of Governors, 17 Sep 2026)
sources.supports: final text: prohibited uses, mandatory labelling cases, no-label cases, label wording, effective 3 months after publication

sources.title: ASCI: Draft Guidelines for Responsible Labelling of Synthetically Generated Content in Advertising (8 May 2026)
sources.supports: draft consulted May-June 2026

sources.title: MediaNews4U (trade press, 29 Sep 2026): ASCI issues guidelines for labelling AI-generated content in advertising
sources.supports: final guidelines released after consultation

items.note: FINAL text signed 17 Sep 2026; 'shall come into effect on the expiration of 3 months from the date of their publication', i.e. about mid/late Dec 2026 (ASCI PDF read 2026-10-04). Rules: (1) banned even with a label: AI-fabricated endorsements or testimonials attributed to real people, AI before-after or result visuals that exaggerate product results, fake locations or facilities shown as real, deepfakes or anyone's likeness without consent, unauthorised copyrighted work (clause 1). (2) Label required: AI influencers/ambassadors, a real person's face or voice replicated even with consent for personalised messages, fabricated events or settings that affect understanding of performance, products that do not exist yet, AI sound effects tied to a core feature, and sponsored AI chatbot recommendations ('Sponsored by [Brand]') (clause 2). (3) Labels: platform labels or wording such as 'Audio/Video created using AI' / 'Audio/Video enhanced using AI' (clause 4). (4) No label: colour/light/noise fixes, decorative backgrounds and jingles, obvious fantasy, AI-generated or AI-enhanced ad COPY, subtitles and translations (clause 3).

items.name: CCPA Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements for Misleading Advertisements, 2022 (Consumer Protection Act, 2019)
items.one_line: Binding Indian rules under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 for every ad in any medium: truthful, substantiated claims; honest 'free' offers; disclaimers that clarify but never contradict; no surrogate ads; endorsements that reflect genuine use and disclose material connections.

sources.title: Gazette of India: CCPA notification dated 9 June 2022, Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements for Misleading Advertisements, 2022
sources.supports: full text: clauses 4 (valid ads), 5 (bait), 6 (surrogate), 7 (free claims), 8 (children), 11 (disclaimers), 12 (duties), 13 (endorser due diligence), 14 (material connection)

sources.title: CCPA: Guidelines and Advisories
sources.supports: list of CCPA guidelines currently published

items.note: In force since notification on 9 June 2022, issued under section 18 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (gazette PDF read 2026-10-04). Rules: (1) objectively factual claims and comparisons must be capable of substantiation; cite source and date when a claim rests on research (cl. 12(a)-(b)). (2) 'Free' only if the consumer pays nothing beyond unavoidable response/delivery cost; no 'free trial' for money-back offers (cl. 7). (3) No vague 'up to' or 'prices from as low as' framing for guarantees and prices; state the fixed period or price (cl. 12(e)(i)). (4) Disclaimers: same language and same font as the claim, in sync with a voice-over, and they may clarify but must not contradict the claim or hide material information (cl. 11). (5) No surrogate or indirect ads for products whose ads are banned (cl. 6). (6) Endorsements must reflect the endorser's genuine, reasonably current opinion based on adequate information or experience, and any material connection must be fully disclosed (cl. 13-14). Obvious humour or hyperbole is allowed if clearly not literal (proviso to cl. 12). Penalty amounts sit in the Act: not quoted here.

items.name: Department of Consumer Affairs 'Endorsement Know-hows!' for celebrities, influencers and virtual influencers (2023)
items.one_line: Government of India guide: celebrities, influencers and virtual influencers must disclose any material connection in simple words like 'advertisement', 'sponsored' or 'paid promotion', and should not endorse what they have not used or checked.

sources.title: PIB (20 Jan 2023): Centre releases endorsement guidelines for Celebs and Social Media Influencers
sources.supports: release date, what counts as material connection, disclosure wording, due diligence

sources.title: Department of Consumer Affairs: Endorsement Know-hows! (PDF)
sources.supports: the guide itself (download failed in this harvest; content taken from the PIB release)

items.note: Released 20 Jan 2023 by the Department of Consumer Affairs under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (PIB, read 2026-10-04). Rules: (1) disclose any material connection: money, trips or hotel stays, media barters, coverage and awards, free products with or without conditions, discounts, gifts, and any family, personal or employment relationship (PIB). (2) Disclosures must be prominent and 'extremely hard to miss' (PIB). (3) Use simple, clear words such as 'advertisement', 'sponsored' or 'paid promotion' (PIB). (4) Do not endorse a product or service you have not personally used or experienced or on which you have not done due diligence (PIB). Applies to virtual influencers too.

items.name: CCPA Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023
items.one_line: Bans 13 specified dark patterns on platforms selling in India, several of them pure copy problems: false urgency, confirm shaming, disguised ads, trick questions, nagging, bait and switch, drip pricing.

sources.title: Gazette of India (30 Nov 2023): Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023
sources.supports: definitions and illustrations in Annexure 1

sources.title: CCPA: Guidelines and Advisories
sources.supports: guidelines in force; separate advisory asking e-commerce platforms to self-audit for dark patterns

items.note: Notified 30 Nov 2023 under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (gazette PDF read 2026-10-04); applies to platforms, advertisers and sellers. Copy rules from Annexure 1: (1) False urgency: no fake scarcity or popularity ('Only 2 rooms left! 30 others are looking at this right now' is the gazette's own illustration) and no fake time-limited 'exclusive' sales. (2) Confirm shaming: no guilt or fear lines on the decline button (gazette examples: 'I will stay unsecured', 'charity is for rich, I don't care'). (3) Disguised advertisement: ads must not pose as user content or news articles; the seller or advertiser must disclose that content is an ad. (4) Trick questions: no double negatives or confusing opt-out wording. (5) Nagging: no repeated asks for app download, phone number or notifications without a way to say no. Also: bait and switch, drip pricing, basket sneaking, forced action, subscription trap, interface interference.

items.name: CCPA Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisement in Coaching Sector, 2024
items.one_line: Ed-tech and coaching ads may not promise guaranteed selection, ranks, marks or jobs, must disclose the topper's rank, course and whether it was paid, and need the student's written consent to use their name or photo.

sources.title: CCPA notification (13 Nov 2024): Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisement in Coaching Sector, 2024
sources.supports: clauses 3 (misleading claims) and 4 (obligations, consent for topper photos)

items.note: Notified 13 Nov 2024 (CCPA PDF read 2026-10-04). Rules: (1) no false claims of selections, rank or success rate, and no 'guaranteed selection', job security, promotion, salary increase or admission promises (cl. 3). (2) When a successful candidate appears, disclose rank secured, name and duration of the course, and whether the course was paid (cl. 4(1)(a)). (3) Disclaimers in the same font as the claim, displayed prominently (cl. 4(1)(b)). (4) No name, photo, testimonial or video of a successful candidate without written consent taken after selection (cl. 4(2)). (5) No false urgency or false popularity (cl. 3(e)).

items.name: Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025: ban on advertising online money games
items.one_line: No person may make or be involved in any ad, in any media, that directly or indirectly promotes an online money game (fantasy, rummy, poker or any stake-based game, skill or chance).

sources.title: MeitY: The Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 (Act text, President's assent and gazette 22.08.2025)
sources.supports: section 6 advertisement prohibition, section 9(2) punishment, section 1(3) commencement by notification

items.note: Act published in the gazette 22 Aug 2025; it comes into force on the date the Central Government notifies (s.1(3)); the commencement notification itself was not read in this harvest, so confirm it is in force before citing a date (status unconfirmed, 2026-10-04). Rules: (1) s.6: 'No person shall make, cause to be made, aid, abet, induce, or otherwise be involved in the making' of any ad in any media 'which directly or indirectly promotes or induces any person to play any online money game'. That covers influencer reels, referral codes, affiliate links and surrogate content for real-money apps. (2) s.9(2): contravening s.6 is punishable with imprisonment up to two years or fine up to fifty lakh rupees or both. (3) E-sports and free online social games are the permitted categories; check the game is not a money game before writing.

items.name: SEBI restrictions on association with unregistered finfluencers (Intermediaries Amendment Regulations 2024 + circular of 29 Jan 2025, updated 8 May 2026)
items.one_line: SEBI-regulated brokers, AMCs, advisers and exchanges may not pay, refer or otherwise associate with anyone who gives securities advice or return/performance claims without SEBI registration; 'education' content must not use recent price data to talk about specific stocks.

sources.title: SEBI circular SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD-1/P/CIR/2025/11 dated 29 Jan 2025, updated on 8 May 2026
sources.supports: regulations gazetted 29 Aug 2024; two prohibited activities; education exemption; FAQ 8 price-data rule changed from three months to thirty days on 8 May 2026

sources.title: SEBI: Details/clarifications on provisions related to association of persons regulated by the Board, MIIs and their agents with persons engaged in prohibited activities
sources.supports: circular landing page

items.note: Regulations gazetted 29 Aug 2024; clarifying circular 29 Jan 2025, updated 8 May 2026 (SEBI PDF read 2026-10-04). Rules: (1) a SEBI-regulated client cannot sponsor, pay, refer clients to, or otherwise associate with a creator who (i) gives advice or recommendations on securities without SEBI registration or (ii) makes express or implied claims of returns or performance without permission (para 2). (2) Pure investor education is exempt, but per FAQ 8 as revised on 8 May 2026 an educator must not use market price data of the preceding THIRTY DAYS (earlier: three months) to name a security, even by code name, in a way that indicates future price, advice or recommendation. (3) For a broker or AMC brief: no 'returns' or 'performance' claims in creator scripts, and the creator's SEBI registration (if any) goes upfront, per ASCI Addendum II (comp:asci_influencer).

items.name: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: defamation (s.356), promoting enmity (s.196), outraging religious feelings (s.299), statements conducing to public mischief (s.353)
items.one_line: India's criminal code sections that satire, political and commentary copy must clear: defamation with its good-faith opinion exceptions, and the offences for promoting group enmity, insulting religion and spreading alarming falsehoods.

sources.title: Ministry of Home Affairs: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (No. 45 of 2023, Act text)
sources.supports: text of ss.196, 299, 353 and 356 with Explanations and Exceptions

sources.title: India Code: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
sources.supports: official statute database entry (PDF timed out for the fetch client)

items.note: BNS (Act 45 of 2023, assented 25 Dec 2023) replaced the IPC; section numbers below read from the Act text on 2026-10-04 (the PRS Bill PDF uses DIFFERENT clause numbers, do not cite it). Rules: (1) s.356(1) defamation = any spoken, written or visual imputation about a person made intending or knowing it will harm their reputation; it can cover a company or group (Expl. 2) and a deceased person (Expl. 1). s.356(2): simple imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both, or community service. (2) Satire and commentary live inside the Exceptions: true imputation for the public good (Exc. 1); good-faith opinion on a public servant's public conduct (Exc. 2) or on anyone's conduct on a public question (Exc. 3), 'and no further' than that conduct; good-faith opinion on a work submitted to public judgment (Exc. 6). So attack the act, the vote, the policy, the speech; never invent facts or private-life allegations. (3) s.196: no words or visuals promoting enmity between religious, racial, language, regional, caste or community groups. (4) s.299: no deliberate, malicious insult to a religion or religious beliefs (up to three years). (5) s.353: no false statement, rumour or report likely to cause public fear or alarm. Criminal defamation is a live risk for political satire pages in India.

items.name: Google Ads Editorial policy (capitalisation, punctuation and symbols, repetition, spacing, style and spelling)
items.one_line: Google Ads text must read like clean, informational search copy: no gimmicky caps, symbols, repetition or spacing, no phone numbers in ad text, correct spelling and grammar, and the advertiser named.

sources.title: Google Advertising Policies Help: Editorial
sources.supports: list of disallowed editorial practices

items.note: Current policy page read 2026-10-04. Not allowed: (1) 'Capitalization that isn't used correctly or for its intended purpose' (no FREE, BUY NOW). (2) 'Punctuation or symbols that aren't used correctly or for their intended purpose' and invalid characters. (3) 'Non-standard, gimmicky, or unnecessary repetition of names, words, or phrases', and repeating text across assets in the same ad group. (4) 'Omitting a space or adding extra spaces'. (5) Phone numbers in ad text; ads not using commonly accepted spelling or grammar or inconsistent with 'the clear and informational presentation style' of Search; business name field must be the domain or recognised advertiser name, with no promotional language. Each sub-policy has its own detail page: open it when a specific symbol or exclamation rule matters (not read here).

items.name: Google Ads Misrepresentation policy
items.one_line: Google Ads bans ads that hide or misstate who the advertiser is, use dishonest pricing, clickbait or fear of negative life events, mimic system dialogs, or promise improbable results as the likely outcome.

sources.title: Google Advertising Policies Help: Misrepresentation
sources.supports: sub-policies: misleading representation, dishonest pricing, clickbait, misleading ad design, manipulated media, unreliable claims, unavailable offers

items.note: Current policy page read 2026-10-04. Rules: (1) no misleading statements or omissions about identity, affiliations or qualifications. (2) No pricing that creates 'a false or misleading impression of the cost'. (3) No 'clickbait tactics or sensationalist text or imagery', and no use of 'negative life events such as death, accidents, illness, arrests or bankruptcy' to pressure immediate action. (4) No ad design that hides that it is an ad: fake buttons, fake system notifications, ad/landing-page mismatch. (5) No 'claims that entice the user with an improbable result (even if this result is possible) as the likely outcome'. (6) No manipulated media to deceive.

items.name: Google Election Ads policy and advertiser verification (incl. India)
items.one_line: Anyone running election ads on Google Ads or YouTube must first pass Google's Election Ads verification; ads then carry 'paid for by' disclosure and enter Google's transparency report.

sources.title: Google Advertising Policies Help: Apply for Election Ads verification
sources.supports: verification required before running Election Ads; false information leads to revocation and suspension

sources.title: Google Advertising Policies Help: Political content
sources.supports: country-specific election ads rules, including India (not read in this harvest)

items.note: Verification page read 2026-10-04: 'Google requires verification for advertisers who want to run Election Ads using Google Ads and Display & Video 360'; false information means revoked verification and possible suspension. India-specific rules (historically including the ECI/MCMC pre-certificate) sit on the Political content page, not read here: confirm before a campaign. Also needs comp:eci_mcc certification during elections.

items.name: LinkedIn Advertising Policies
items.one_line: LinkedIn ads must be truthful with factual support for claims, disclose partnerships, avoid misleading health claims, and follow 'standard text' rules; political ads and affiliate ads are prohibited.

sources.title: LinkedIn: Advertising Policies
sources.supports: prohibited content (political, affiliate, health claims, fraud and deception) and standard text rule

items.note: Current policy page read 2026-10-04. Rules: (1) 'Any claims in your ad must have factual support'; no deceptive claims about competitors; do not imply endorsement without permission; 'disclose any pertinent partnerships'. (2) 'Political ads are prohibited', including ads for or against a candidate, party, law or regulation. (3) 'Ads related to affiliate advertising are prohibited.' (4) No 'unrealistic or misleading claims about health improvements', incl. diet and weight loss. (5) Standard Text: no 'incorrect spelling, grammar, punctuation, excessive emojis, capitalization or unrelated hashtags'.

items.name: Meta labelling of AI-generated and manipulated content ('AI info')
items.one_line: Facebook, Instagram and Threads add 'AI info' labels when they detect industry AI indicators or the uploader discloses AI; high-risk deceptive media gets a more prominent label; content that breaks other rules is removed regardless of AI.

sources.title: Meta Newsroom (Apr 2024, updated Jul and Sep 2024): Our Approach to Labeling AI-Generated Content and Manipulated Media
sources.supports: AI info labels, detection via industry indicators, self-disclosure, prominent labels for high-risk content, label moved to menu for AI-edited content

items.note: Policy announced Apr 2024 with updates in Jul 2024 (label renamed 'AI info') and later in 2024 (AI-edited content label moved to the post menu) (Meta newsroom read 2026-10-04). Rules: (1) disclose AI-generated video, audio or images at upload using Meta's tool; Meta also labels from C2PA/IPTC-style indicators. (2) If altered media creates 'a particularly high risk of materially deceiving the public on a matter of importance', Meta may add a more prominent label. (3) AI does not excuse rule-breaking: content violating Community Standards is removed whoever made it.

items.name: UK CAP Code (Non-broadcast Advertising) and ASA influencer guidance
items.one_line: UK ads, including influencer posts and advertorials, must be obviously identifiable as marketing; they must not mislead and claims need evidence; the ASA enforces it.

sources.title: ASA/CAP: CAP Code section 02 Recognition of marketing communications
sources.supports: rules 2.1, 2.3, 2.4 and the link to DMCCA Schedule 20

sources.title: ASA/CAP and CMA: Influencers' guide to making clear that ads are ads
sources.supports: influencer disclosure guidance (first edition 28 Sep 2018, second 2 Feb 2020)

items.note: In force (CAP Code page read 2026-10-04). Rules: (1) rule 2.1: 'Marketing communications must be obviously identifiable as such'; unsolicited marketing email must be identifiable as marketing without opening it. (2) rule 2.3: marketers must not falsely claim or imply they act as a consumer, and must make commercial intent clear: an influencer post for a brand needs an upfront label such as 'Ad'. (3) rule 2.4: advertorials must be clearly marked, e.g. 'advertisement feature'. (4) Rules 2.3 and 2.4 reflect prohibited practices in Schedule 20 of the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (CAP note), so breach can also be a statutory issue. Misleading-claims and substantiation rules are in CAP section 3 (not read here).

items.name: UK Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations (PECR) regulation 22: email and text marketing
items.one_line: In the UK you may not send marketing emails or texts to individuals without specific consent, except the 'soft opt-in' for your own existing customers about similar products, and every message needs your identity and an opt-out.

sources.title: ICO: Guide to PECR, Electronic mail marketing
sources.supports: regulation 22 summary, soft opt-in conditions, identity and contact address

items.note: In force (ICO guide read 2026-10-04). Rules: (1) 'You must not send marketing emails or texts to individuals without specific consent.' (2) Soft opt-in only for people who bought or negotiated to buy a similar product from you and were given a simple opt-out when their details were collected and in every message; never for bought-in lists. (3) 'You must not disguise or conceal your identity', and provide a valid contact address for opt-outs. B2B emails to corporate addresses follow lighter rules (see ICO). EU equivalent: ePrivacy Directive 2002/58/EC Art 13 with GDPR consent (not harvested here).

items.name: EU Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065) Article 26: advertising transparency on online platforms
items.one_line: On EU online platforms every ad must be identifiable as an ad in real time, showing on whose behalf it runs, who paid, and the main targeting parameters; platforms must let users declare their posts as commercial communications.

sources.title: EUR-Lex: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (Digital Services Act)
sources.supports: Article 26 text

items.note: DSA obligations for online platforms apply since 17 Feb 2024 (EUR-Lex text read 2026-10-04 for Art 26; date of application from Art 93, not re-read). Rules: (1) ads shown to EU users must be clearly identifiable as ads, with the advertiser and payer named (Art 26(1)). (2) Platforms must offer a function for users to declare that their content is or contains commercial communications, and then label it (Art 26(2)): for an EU-facing influencer post, switch on the platform's paid-partnership tool. (3) No ads targeted on special-category data such as religion or political opinions (Art 26(3)).

items.name: FTC Health Products Compliance Guidance (health claim substantiation)
items.one_line: Any US health or wellness claim must be backed by 'competent and reliable scientific evidence', generally randomized controlled human trials, judged on the net impression the ad leaves.

sources.title: FTC: Health Products Compliance Guidance
sources.supports: substantiation standard, RCTs, net impression of disclosures, testimonials and expert endorsements

items.note: Current FTC guidance page read 2026-10-04 (issued Dec 2022). Rules: (1) health-benefit claims must meet 'competent and reliable scientific evidence'; 'Randomized, controlled human clinical trials (RCTs) are the most reliable form of evidence' and generally what experts require. (2) What counts is what reasonable consumers take away, not what the marketer meant ('consumer-driven' ad meaning). (3) A disclosure fails if 'a significant minority of consumers' still take a misleading claim from the ad (net impression). (4) Testimonials and expert endorsements do not substitute for evidence (guidance section on testimonials). Indian equivalents: comp:ccpa_misleading_ads_2022 and the ASCI Code.

items.name: US Copyright Office: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence report (Part 2 Copyrightability, 2025)
items.one_line: US copyright protects human authorship; purely AI-generated output is not protected, so AI-drafted copy a client wants to own needs real human creative contribution.

sources.title: U.S. Copyright Office: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
sources.supports: Part 1 digital replicas (31 Jul 2024), Part 2 copyrightability of generative-AI outputs (29 Jan 2025), Part 3 training (pre-publication 9 May 2025)

items.note: Part 2 published 29 Jan 2025 (USCO page read 2026-10-04). The landing page states only that Part 2 'addresses the copyrightability of outputs created using generative AI'; its conclusion (human authorship required; prompts alone generally insufficient) was not re-read in the report itself here: medium confidence. Practical rules: (1) tell clients that unedited AI output may not be ownable; keep drafts showing human selection, arrangement and rewriting. (2) Never present AI output as 'original copyright work' in a contract without that human contribution. (3) Part 1 (digital replicas) is the US reference for AI voice and likeness clones: get written consent for any real person's voice or face.

items.name: Associated Press standards around generative AI (newsroom AI disclosure norm)
items.one_line: A benchmark newsroom policy: AP staff do not use generative AI to create publishable content, treat AI output as unvetted source material, and do not transmit AI images that falsely depict reality.

sources.title: Associated Press: Standards around generative AI
sources.supports: no AI for publishable content, AI output as unvetted source material, AI image rules

items.note: AP's published standard (first issued Aug 2023; page read 2026-10-04). Use as the norm for news, explainer and political-information copy: (1) AP staff 'do not use it to create publishable content'. (2) 'Any output from a generative AI tool should be treated as unvetted source material': every AI-suggested fact, quote or number gets verified against a primary source before publishing. (3) AP will not transmit AI-generated images 'suspected or proven to be false depictions of reality'; an AI illustration that is itself the news may run only if clearly labelled. Pair with comp:eu_ai_act_art50 (public-interest text disclosure in the EU) and comp:it_rules_sgi_2026 (India).

items.name: Meta branded content policies and the 'Paid partnership' label (Instagram, Facebook)
items.one_line: Creators posting content for a brand in exchange for something of value must tag the business partner with Meta's paid partnership tool; in India ASCI accepts the Instagram 'Paid Partnership' tag as a disclosure label.

sources.title: ASCI Guidelines for Influencer Advertising in Digital Media
sources.supports: '"Paid Partnership" tag on Instagram' is a permitted disclosure label (1.3a); platform tools are in addition to the creator's own disclosure (1.2d)

sources.title: Meta Transparency Center: Advertising Standards
sources.supports: Meta's ad and branded content policy hub (page could not be read by fetch tools: HTTP 400/404)

items.note: STATUS NOT CONFIRMED from Meta's own page: transparency.meta.com and facebook.com help pages refused the fetch tools on 2026-10-04 (HTTP 400/404). What is sourced: (1) ASCI lists the Instagram 'Paid Partnership' tag as a permitted label (ASCI 1.3a). (2) ASCI and the FTC both say a platform tool should be used in ADDITION to the creator's own clear label, not instead of it (ASCI 1.2d; comp:ftc_endorsement_guides). Before writing to Meta's specific rules (prohibited branded content, political branded content), read Meta's branded content policy page in a browser.
